traditional.text: And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.

ait.text: And I in turn tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not overpower it.

note.text: The nearly universal rendering is “church,” and readers know what it refers to. A first-century hearer, however, knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Greek Old Testament’s term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” now suggests a building or an institution, so “assembly” is used throughout this translation.

traditional.text: Therefore when thou doest thine alms, do not sound a trumpet before thee, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may have glory of men. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.

ait.text: So when you give to the needy, do not sound a trumpet ahead of you, as the performers do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that they may be praised by people. Truly I tell you, they have been paid their reward in full.

note.text: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a stage actor, and in this passage the picture of a performance is active: a trumpet, street corners, an audience. Jewish Greek before the New Testament already used the word for a godless or insincere person, which is why most translations have “hypocrites” here. “Performers” is used in verses 2, 5 and 16 because the charge in each case is doing religion in order to be seen.

traditional.text: The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.

ait.text: The lamp of the body is the eye. So if your eye is generous, your whole body will be full of light;

note.text: The Greek word means single or sincere, and related words are used of open-handed giving. The saying stands between treasure in heaven and slavery to wealth, and it is paired with the “evil eye”, a known idiom for stinginess, so “generous” fits the context. Most translations have “healthy” or “sound”, keeping the physical picture of an eye that lets in light, and mention generosity in a footnote; that picture is less visible in this rendering.

traditional.text: And saying, Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.

ait.text: and saying, “Turn back, for the kingdom of the heavens has come near.”

note.text: The traditional rendering is “repent,” which most translations keep as an established term. In modern English “repent” centers on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word, as used in the Gospels, carries the prophets’ call to return to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct. The related noun in verses 8 and 11 is rendered “turning back.”

traditional.text: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

ait.text: In the beginning was the Logos, and the Logos was with God, and the Logos was God.

note.text: Nearly all translations render this “Word.” The Greek term covered speech, message, account and reason, and to many Greek-speaking readers it also suggested the rational principle that orders the world. Most scholars think John’s main background is the Hebrew Bible: God’s creating speech in Genesis 1, the “word of the Lord,” and the figure of Wisdom, which “Word” reflects and “Logos” does not. The Greek term is kept here as a title because “the Word” in current English usually means the Bible, which would give “the Word was God” a false sense.
